blocks.text: Warm greetings, Tauck friends!
“Xin chào” — welcome to Hanoi!

I am absolutely delighted to begin this 16-day journey through Vietnam, Cambodia, and Thailand with you. My name is Xavier Brunelle, and I have the pleasure of being your Tauck Tour Director for this adventure. You can simply call me X — it makes things a little easier!

I hope you will find comfort at the Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi, an iconic landmark where French colonial architecture, Vietnamese heritage, and more than 120 years of history come together in a living symbol of the city’s transformation. The hotel offers several dining options, each providing its own way to discover the local culture. I have also put together a selection of restaurants and cafés around town for you to explore, along with a curated Google Maps list to help you find your way. Simply scan the QR code at the bottom of this page.

Eating out in Hanoi can be a wonderful and generally safe experience when you choose carefully. You can follow my recommendations, ask the hotel concierge for advice, or look for busy food stalls where a steady flow of customers means fresh food is being prepared regularly. In Vietnam, one of the most delightful ways to begin discovering a country — and flirting with its history — is through the taste of its food.

The Metropole itself has a fascinating story to tell. If you have the opportunity, I highly recommend joining the hotel’s historical tour, which takes place each afternoon and must be booked in advance through the Concierge desk.

In this welcome package, you will find your itinerary, the guest information form, the Vespa tour waiver, menus selections, and additional information to help you make the most of your time in Hanoi. Should you need any assistance or further information, please do not hesitate to contact the hotel’s Majordome (Concierge) or reach out to me directly by email or WhatsApp.
Email: xbrunelle@tauck.com · WhatsApp: +46 70 549 7222
Our First Meeting

Please bring the following completed paperwork and documents to our hospitality desk on Day 1, between 9:00 and 11:00 a.m., in the Business Center. The hotel staff can confirm the location should it change.

1. Completed guest information form
2. Signed Vespa tour waiver
3. Printed color copy of your Cambodian visa
4. Your Vietnamese visa
5. Your passport
6. Your three menu choices, completed
A Journey to Remember

Ahead of us lie busy days, new experiences, unfamiliar flavors and fragrances, and a rich mosaic of cultures and histories. We will encounter stories of resilience, traditions that have endured for centuries, and perspectives that may stay with us long after we return home.

As with any journey, our schedule may occasionally change along the way. Flexibility is part of the adventure, so expect the unexpected! My role is to take care of the details, anticipate challenges, and manage the unexpected so that you can relax and enjoy the experience. You are here to discover, learn, taste, explore, and make wonderful memories. Let me take care of the rest.

Bring your curiosity, your adventurous spirit, and an open mind. Together, we will make these 16 days more than just a journey through three beautiful countries. We will make them a shared experience, full of discovery, connection, and memories to cherish. Always be prepared to embrace the unexpected, those are often the real memories that says….

I look forward to traveling with you!
Warmly,
Xavier (X)

Recommended reading & viewing
Books, cinema and cultural series for Vietnam, Cambodia & Thailand, from the supplied Southeast Asia Reading and Viewing Guide.
Books (7)
The Things They Carried
Tim O'Brien (Vietnam)

A groundbreaking masterpiece of war fiction and personal reflection that blurs the lines between memory and truth, capturing the visceral sensory details and emotional baggage of soldiers marching through the Vietnamese countryside.
Bookshop.org
Amazon
Goodreads
Catfish and Mandala: A Two-Wheeled Voyage Through Vietnam
Andrew X. Pham (Vietnam)

A poignant travel memoir chronicling an American-Vietnamese refugee's solo bicycle odyssey across modern Vietnam. Pham confronts memory, diaspora identity, post-war reconstruction, and family history from Saigon to Hanoi.
Bookshop.org
Amazon
Goodreads
The Sympathizer
Viet Thanh Nguyen (Vietnam)

Winner of the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, this sharp, satirical spy novel chronicles the life of a dual-agent army captain navigating the 1975 fall of Saigon, exile in California, and subsequent re-education.
Bookshop.org
Amazon
Goodreads
First They Killed My Father: A Daughter of Cambodia Remembers
Loung Ung (Cambodia)
A devastatingly powerful, intimate child's-eye memoir chronicling the 1975 Khmer Rouge evacuation of Phnom Penh, forced labor camps, survival, and ultimate resilience.
Bookshop.org
Amazon
Goodreads
Angkor and the Khmer Civilization
Michael D. Coe (Cambodia)

The quintessential historical and archaeological introduction to the Khmer Empire. Coe synthesizes inscriptions, hydraulic engineering, religion, and temple architecture, perfect reading before walking Angkor Wat and the Bayon.
Bookshop.org
Amazon
Goodreads
Sightseeing
Rattawut Lapcharoensap (Thailand)

A luminous, award-winning collection of short stories depicting contemporary Thai life—from American tourism clashes in tropical island beach towns to youthful coming-of-age moments in working-class Bangkok.
Bookshop.org
Amazon
Goodreads
A History of Thailand
Chris Baker & Pasuk Phongpaichit (Thailand)

An authoritative, highly engaging single-volume history tracing Thailand from early forest settlements and the Siamese kingdoms of Ayutthaya and Thonburi through modern democratic politics and cultural shifts.
Bookshop.org
Amazon
Goodreads
Films & documentaries (8)
The Quiet American (2002) — Vietnam
Phillip Noyce | Starring Michael Caine, Brendan Fraser

Adapted from Graham Greene's classic novel, this atmospheric political drama portrays Saigon in 1952 during the waning days of the First Indochina War. Filmed extensively on location in Hanoi, Saigon, and Ninh Binh, it offers exceptional historical texture.
Available on Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV
Indochine (1992) — Vietnam
Régis Wargnier | Starring Catherine Deneuve, Vincent Perez

Academy Award winner for Best Foreign Language Film. An epic romantic historical drama set against the twilight of French colonial rubber plantations from the 1930s through 1954, showcasing breathtaking panoramic footage of Ha Long Bay and imperial Hue.
Available on Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV
The Scent of Green Papaya (1993) — Vietnam
Tran Anh Hung

A visually meditative French-Vietnamese film depicting domestic life, traditional culinary rituals, and family dynamics in 1950s Saigon. It serves as a gentle, sensory celebration of Vietnamese home life and cuisine.
Available on Kino Lorber, Amazon Prime Video
The Vietnam War (2017 Mini-series) — Vietnam
Ken Burns & Lynn Novick (10 Episodes)

An extraordinary, balanced documentary masterclass that weaves together archival footage, music, and first-hand testimonies from North Vietnamese soldiers, South Vietnamese fighters, and American veterans.
Available on PBS Passport, Amazon Prime Video
First They Killed My Father (2017) — Cambodia
Angelina Jolie | Produced by Rithy Panh

Filmed entirely in Cambodia in the Khmer language with an all-Cambodian cast, this film faithfully adapts Loung Ung's memoir of childhood survival during the Khmer Rouge reign. A visually striking, deeply respectful production.
Available exclusively on Netflix
The Killing Fields (1984) — Cambodia
Roland Joffé | Starring Sam Waterston, Dr. Haing S. Ngor

The landmark three-time Academy Award-winning historical drama chronicling the real friendship between American journalist Sydney Schanberg and Cambodian photojournalist Dith Pran during the 1975 fall of Phnom Penh.
Available on Apple TV, Amazon Prime Video
The Railway Man (2013) — Thailand
Jonathan Teplitzky | Starring Colin Firth, Nicole Kidman, Hiroyuki Sanada

A moving biographical drama based on the true story of British officer Eric Lomax, who was held as a prisoner of war on the notorious Thai-Burma 'Death Railway' and bridge at Kanchanaburi, exploring enduring trauma and wartime reconciliation.
Available on Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV
Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (2010) — Thailand
Apichatpong Weerasethakul
Winner of the Palme d'Or at Cannes. A hypnotic, artistic cinematic masterpiece that immerses viewers in northeastern Thai spiritual animism, reincarnation, and mystical jungle lore.
Available on Strand Releasing, Kanopy, Amazon Prime Video
Travel, culinary & culture series (5)
Street Food: Asia (Netflix, Season 1)
Key Episodes: Bangkok, Thailand (Episode 1) & Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam (Episode 7)

Produced by the team behind Chef's Table. The Bangkok episode spotlights Supinya Junsuta (Jay Fai) and her crab omelet mastery; the Saigon episode captures sidewalk snail (ốc) culture and broken rice heritage.
Somebody Feed Phil (Netflix)
Key Episodes: Bangkok (S1:E1), Saigon (S1:E2), and Chiang Mai (Season 1)
Lighthearted, joyful culinary exploration. Perfect pre-trip viewing for navigating morning pho stalls, floating markets, and northern Thai khao soi noodle soup traditions.
Anthony Bourdain: Parts Unknown (CNN / Max)
Key Episodes: Hanoi, Vietnam (S8:E1) & Chiang Mai, Thailand (S3:E7)

Features Bourdain's celebrated dinner of bún chả and cold beer with President Barack Obama at Hương Liên in Hanoi, as well as nighttime explorations of northern Thai herbal sausages and night markets.
Luke Nguyen's Vietnam (SBS / Prime Video)
Key Episodes: Comprehensive 10-episode journey from Saigon to the Mekong, Hue, and Hanoi
Intimate, market-level cooking demonstrations highlighting Vietnamese regional herbs, river fish, and age-old culinary techniques right on river barges and village courtyards.
Gordon Ramsay: Uncharted (Disney+ / National Geographic)
Key Episodes: Cambodia (Season 3, Episode 6)
Ramsay travels down the Mekong River and across Tonle Sap lake to explore traditional Khmer curries, freshwater fish traps, and indigenous aromatics.
4-week pre-departure plan
Week 1 (Focus on Vietnam): Read 'The Things They Carried'; Watch 'The Quiet American' and 'Somebody Feed Phil: Saigon'.
Week 2 (Focus on Vietnam): Read 'Catfish and Mandala'; Watch Ken Burns' 'The Vietnam War' (Episodes 1-3) & 'Street Food: Asia (Saigon)'.
Week 3 (Focus on Cambodia): Read 'Angkor and the Khmer Civilization' & 'First They Killed My Father'; Stream 'First They Killed My Father' on Netflix.
Week 4 (Focus on Thailand): Read 'Sightseeing'; Watch 'The Railway Man' and 'Somebody Feed Phil: Bangkok & Chiang Mai'.

AN INVITATION TO OUR TRAVELERS
Help Wondercase Grow

As you travel with Wondercase, tell us what delighted you, what could be simpler, and what you wish it could do. Share a thought whenever it occurs to you—even over breakfast. Your experience can help shape what comes next.
You are our travelers, explorers, storytellers—and co-creators of this new idea.
Shared Photo Gallery coming soon
Download selected journey content

Tap Export a section in the travel book to save one or more days, hotels and flights, guides and resources, or the full itinerary. Each journey day also has Download this day as PDF. Downloads reflect the latest saved schedules and include a Back to app link.
Home and today’s plans

Home and the journey page for today show the same date-specific Xavier announcement. Memory links can be pasted directly into the body text; separate restaurant, website and album fields have been removed. Home has a compact illustrated cover banner in light green and gold tones, followed by Xavier’s announcements and a rounded journey panel with the date and local time together on one line. The panel combines the journey status, date, Day number, title and destination together in an evenly spaced row and a green-and-gold button to open today’s journey. The journey map follows this panel and a green travel-book panel with a matching green-and-gold button. Find Xavier’s contact card at the top of Info, with phone and email side by side; expand About Xavier to read his biography. The shared album is available only in Photos. Each journey day has a shorter, proportionally cropped banner, a Day number beside the introduction, and a clear All 14 days button beneath its Day number and date. Timeline times use larger text; tap a time to enlarge it with its activity details. Close the panel with Close, Escape, or a tap outside it.
Meet your fellow travelers

In Info, guest profiles appear two side by side, each with a photo above the name and hometown, followed by A little about me. Tap a guest’s photo, name, or profile area to open a larger photo, hometown, and approved introduction. An olive-green Introduction available indicator means there is more to read. Email and WhatsApp details are not displayed on guest cards. Open your profile and use Write your own introduction to send your introduction to Xavier for review.
Your journey, hotels, and stories

Each journey day includes its itinerary. Expand How about some trivia? at the bottom of each day to play the daily quiz, or A little language lesson to see vocabulary and pronunciation. Both panels start collapsed. The More… tab has an expandable collection of books, online heritage resources, films and traveler perspectives and five suggested Tauck journeys across Asia, with trip lengths, destinations and links to the official tour pages. Photos opens the shared PhotoCircle album for viewing and adding photos. Tonight’s stay opens the matching hotel in Hotels + Flights. Explore the local guide cards, optional tours, hotel menus, and illustrated destination stories where available. Documents include a return link to the app.
Memories and feedback

Share memories and comments in the journey journal. In Add a memory, write your message and choose Add photos or files, then press Post memory to save everything together. Select up to three JPG, PNG or WebP photos (10 MB before automatic resizing) or PDFs (4 MB each). Keep the page open until saving finishes; selected files are not retained after closing or reloading. Photos open separately and PDFs download, allowing you to return to the app. Only the original posting device can add or remove attachments; deleting a memory also removes its files. In More…, expand Rate the app — share your feedback to complete Kingdoms & Dragons App Feedback. The name defaults to Anonymous and can be changed. The single overall rating starts at zero and accepts half-star ratings from 0 to 5.
Rate: Overall experience with the app
Optional comments: What worked especially well for you? What could be improved? Was there anything you wished the app included? Any other comments or suggestions?

Feedback is shared with fellow travelers. Only the submitting browser/device can edit or delete its feedback, using Edit my feedback or Delete my feedback. Clearing browser data removes that access. Current comments, announcements, and feedback are viewed in the app; this PDF is a downloaded snapshot.
Help and Tour Director access

Installation instructions, the tutorial video with speed controls, and the instruction booklet are at the bottom of Info. Xavier’s authenticated Tour Director access manages announcements, daily timeline changes, guest photo uploads, and introduction approval. When signed in, Xavier can change his own contact-card photo or restore the original. The travel book uses the current photo when opened.

Tap any recommendation to open it in Google Maps. Reservations are especially important for Jumbo Seafood, Keng Eng Kee, Kotuwa, Peach Blossoms, Odette, and HolyCrab.
Xavier’s restaurant recommendations
Song Fa Bak kut teh—peppery pork-rib broth with fried dough sticks. ↗
Jumbo Seafood Singapore seafood institution; chili crab with fried mantou buns. ↗
Keng Eng Kee Seafood Family-run zi char; coffee pork ribs, moonlight hor fun, chili crab, and prawn-paste chicken. ↗
Samy’s Curry North and South Indian cooking; fish-head curry and fish-potato croquettes on a banana-leaf set. ↗
Kotuwa Chef Rishi Naleendra’s Sri Lankan cooking; crab curry, egg hoppers, and mutton rolls. ↗
The Coconut Club Modern nasi lemak with fried chicken, sambal, peanuts, anchovies, and coconut rice. ↗
Peach Blossoms Modern Chinese cuisine and Marina Bay views; steamed carrot cake with lobster, drunken-crab noodles, and the Forbidden Roll. ↗
National Kitchen by Violet Oon Peranakan and Singaporean classics in the National Gallery; dry laksa or beef rendang with sambal eggplant and traditional kueh for dessert. ↗
Hawker centres
Lau Pa Sat Victorian-style market and evening satay street; try skewers and fresh sugar-cane juice. ↗
Albert Centre Market & Food Centre Local Bugis market for chicken rice, fishball noodles, laksa, and ice kacang. ↗
Market Street Hawker Centre Modern two-level centre at CapitaSpring; Ipoh hor fun, truffle wonton mee, and biryani. ↗
Maxwell Food Centre Famous, easy-to-navigate centre; Tian Tian chicken rice or fish-noodle soup. ↗
Coffee, cafés & ice cream
Narrative Coffee Stand Local roasters serving cold brew and espresso-style coffee. ↗
Ya Kun Kaya Toast Kaya toast breakfast sets with local kopi. ↗
Toast Box Singaporean coffee and kaya-toast breakfast sets. ↗
My Awesome Cafe Local vegan café with a vibrant interior, popular for after-work drinks. ↗
Apiary Playful local ice-cream flavors. ↗
Birds of Paradise Gelato Boutique Botanical gelato inspired by herbs, flowers, and Southeast Asian flavors. ↗
Near Raffles
Chin Chin Eating House Old-school Hainanese comfort food and classic chicken rice. ↗
New Ubin Seafood Singaporean seafood and zi char in a lively communal setting. ↗
Un-Yang-Kor-Dai Authentic northeastern Thai cooking. ↗
Odette Modern French tasting menus with optional wine pairing; reservations required. ↗
HolyCrab Playful Singaporean crab dishes; try pepper crab with crispy mantou. ↗
Cocktails & views
Nutmeg & Clove Award-winning cocktails inspired by Singapore’s history and flavors. ↗
LeVeL33 Marina Bay views from a high-rise microbrewery. ↗
Caffe Fernet Italian restaurant and bar overlooking Marina Bay. ↗
Rooftop Bar at Heritage Casual rooftop views of Boat Quay and Marina Bay. ↗
Night Hawk Intimate speakeasy with creative menus and cocktails. ↗
Jigger & Pony Acclaimed cocktail bar celebrated for beautifully executed classics. ↗
Bar KAP Teochew-inspired cocktails in a historic mansion setting. ↗

questions.question: Which city welcomes us at the start of this tour?
questions.fact: Our itinerary begins in Hanoi, Vietnam’s capital, with a welcome reception and dinner.

questions.question: Which historic hotel is our Hanoi home?
questions.fact: The Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi is our base for the first two nights.

questions.question: Hanoi is the capital of which country?
questions.fact: Hanoi is Vietnam’s capital; later in the tour we visit Cambodia and Thailand.

questions.question: Which restaurant hosts our welcome dinner?
questions.fact: Our first evening’s dinner is at Le Beaulieu in the Metropole Hanoi.

questions.question: Hanoi’s water puppetry grew out of traditions associated with which landscape?
questions.fact: Water puppetry developed in the villages of northern Vietnam’s Red River Delta, where flooded fields provided a stage.

questions.question: The Hanoi Hilton was a nickname for which place on our sightseeing route?
questions.fact: Hoa Lo Prison is widely known by the wartime nickname Hanoi Hilton; it is part of our Hanoi sightseeing day.

questions.question: What flower does the One Pillar Pagoda’s design evoke?
questions.fact: The small pagoda rises from a single pillar above a pond, evoking a lotus blossom.

questions.question: Whose mausoleum is included in our Hanoi sightseeing?
questions.fact: The itinerary includes Ho Chi Minh’s Mausoleum alongside the Presidential Palace and One Pillar Pagoda.

questions.question: Which Vietnamese city was the imperial capital of the Nguyen dynasty?
questions.fact: Hue served as the Nguyen dynasty’s imperial capital and contains the citadel and imperial monuments we visit.

questions.question: Which emperor’s mausoleum do we visit on the way to Hue?
questions.fact: After landing in Da Nang, our itinerary takes us to Emperor Tu Duc’s mausoleum before the hotel in Hue.

questions.question: Which enclosed royal area lies within Hue’s Imperial City?
questions.fact: The Purple Forbidden City formed the innermost royal precinct of the imperial complex in Hue.

questions.question: What is a cyclo, used for our Hue tour?
questions.fact: A cyclo is a pedal-powered, three-wheeled passenger vehicle; we use them to explore Hue.

questions.question: Which river do we cruise after visiting Thien Mu Pagoda?
questions.fact: Our Hue morning pairs Thien Mu Pagoda with a cruise on the Perfume River.

questions.question: Thien Mu Pagoda is a landmark of which city?
questions.fact: Thien Mu Pagoda stands beside the Perfume River in Hue.

questions.question: Which resort is our lunch stop between Hue and Da Nang?
questions.fact: The itinerary stops for lunch at Horizon restaurant in Vedana Lagoon Resort before continuing to Da Nang.

questions.question: Where do we stay after arriving in Da Nang?
questions.fact: Furama Resort is our coastal base for Da Nang and the excursion to Hoi An.

questions.question: Hoi An’s historic town is especially associated with which former role?
questions.fact: Hoi An flourished as a trading port, and its old town reflects Vietnamese and international influences.

questions.question: Which organization recognizes Hoi An Ancient Town as a World Heritage Site?
questions.fact: UNESCO recognizes Hoi An Ancient Town for its well-preserved historic trading-port character.

questions.question: Which activity comes before our visit to Hoi An?
options: A visit to a local farming village
questions.fact: Our itinerary begins with a local farming village before continuing to Hoi An.

questions.question: What type of transport helps us explore Hoi An’s old town?
questions.fact: The itinerary includes a transfer onto cyclos to see Hoi An’s historic streets.

questions.question: What is Saigon’s official name today?
questions.fact: Ho Chi Minh City is still widely called Saigon, the name used throughout our itinerary.

questions.question: The Cu Chi tunnels are best described as what?
options: An underground network used during wartime
A natural cave system beneath Angkor
questions.fact: The Cu Chi tunnels formed an underground network with passageways and facilities used during the wars in Vietnam.

questions.question: Which part of Vietnam is home to the Cu Chi tunnels?
questions.fact: Cu Chi lies outside Ho Chi Minh City in southern Vietnam; we visit after our flight from Da Nang.

questions.question: Which hotel becomes our base in Saigon?
questions.fact: After visiting Cu Chi, we arrive at Park Hyatt Saigon, our base for the city sights and evening Vespa tour.

questions.question: Which market is on our Saigon city sightseeing route?
questions.fact: The itinerary includes Ben Thanh Market, one of Ho Chi Minh City’s best-known landmarks.

questions.question: Saigon’s former Presidential Palace is also commonly known by which name?
questions.fact: The former Presidential Palace is also called Independence Palace or Reunification Palace.

questions.question: Which historic civic building is on our Saigon city tour?
questions.fact: The Saigon city tour includes the historic Central Post Office alongside Ben Thanh market and the former Presidential Palace.

questions.question: What vehicle is featured in our Saigon evening food tour?
questions.fact: Our evening itinerary explores Saigon’s food and nightlights by Vespa.

questions.question: Which Cambodian city is our base for exploring Angkor?
questions.fact: We fly from Saigon to Siem Reap, the gateway to the Angkor temple sites.

questions.question: Which temple on our afternoon tour is famous for trees growing through its ruins?
questions.fact: Ta Prohm is famous for large tree roots entwined with its stone ruins and appeared in the Tomb Raider film.

questions.question: What is Bayon temple especially known for?
options: A single pillar above a pond
questions.fact: Bayon, within Angkor Thom, is celebrated for its towers bearing large carved faces.

questions.question: Angkor Thom was what kind of place?
questions.fact: Angkor Thom was a royal city of the Khmer Empire; Bayon stands near its center.

questions.question: Angkor Wat was originally dedicated to which Hindu deity?
questions.fact: Angkor Wat was built in the 12th century as a temple dedicated to Vishnu and later became a Buddhist site.

questions.question: Which empire built Angkor Wat?
questions.fact: Angkor Wat is one of the great architectural achievements of the Khmer Empire.

questions.question: Which lake do we explore after our sunrise visit to Angkor Wat?
questions.fact: After Angkor Wat and breakfast, the itinerary takes us by private boat onto Tonle Sap.

questions.question: What is unusual about the river connecting Tonle Sap to the Mekong?
questions.fact: Seasonal changes in the Mekong’s water level reverse the Tonle Sap River’s flow, expanding and draining the lake.

questions.question: Chiang Mai is in which part of Thailand?
questions.fact: We fly via Bangkok to Chiang Mai in northern Thailand and tour its Old Walled City.

questions.question: What does the name Chiang Mai mean?
questions.fact: Chiang Mai means new city; it was founded in 1296 as a capital of the Lanna kingdom.

questions.question: Which features still mark Chiang Mai’s historic Old City?
questions.fact: Surviving walls, gates and a surrounding moat trace Chiang Mai’s historic city boundary.

questions.question: Which historic kingdom is closely associated with Chiang Mai?
questions.fact: Chiang Mai was a capital of the Lanna kingdom, whose heritage remains visible in northern Thai culture and architecture.

questions.question: Which sanctuary is on our Chiang Mai itinerary?
questions.fact: Our itinerary visits Kanta Elephant Sanctuary before lunch and the Mae Rim village visit.

questions.question: Which elephant species is native to Thailand?
questions.fact: Thailand’s native elephants are Asian elephants, a species found across parts of South and Southeast Asia.

questions.question: An elephant’s trunk combines which two body parts?
questions.fact: An elephant’s trunk is an elongated nose and upper lip, used for breathing, smelling, touching and handling food.

questions.question: Which village area follows the elephant sanctuary in our itinerary?
questions.fact: After the sanctuary lunch, we visit the Mae Rim Hill Tribe Village in the Chiang Mai area.

questions.question: Doi Suthep temple overlooks which city?
questions.fact: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep stands on the mountain above Chiang Mai, our base for three nights.

questions.question: What does wat mean in Thai place names?
questions.fact: Wat refers to a temple or monastery, as in Wat Phra That Doi Suthep, Wat Arun and Wat Pho.

questions.question: What is the gleaming central sacred structure at Doi Suthep called?
questions.fact: The temple’s golden chedi is a Buddhist reliquary monument, also known as a stupa.

questions.question: Which mythical serpents decorate the famous staircase at Doi Suthep?
questions.fact: Nagas are serpent beings found in Buddhist and Hindu traditions; they flank Doi Suthep’s ceremonial staircase.

questions.question: Bangkok is commonly called Krung Thep in Thai. What does this mean?
questions.fact: Krung Thep is a shortened form of Bangkok’s ceremonial Thai name and means city of angels.

questions.question: Which urban transport system do we try on arrival in Bangkok?
questions.fact: Our first Bangkok afternoon includes a ride on the BTS Skytrain, an elevated urban rail system.

questions.question: Which hotel is our base in Bangkok?
questions.fact: Rosewood Bangkok is our base for the final nights and the farewell celebrations.

questions.question: What is Thailand’s currency?
questions.fact: The baht is Thailand’s currency; dong and riel belong to the two countries we visited earlier on the tour.

questions.question: Which Bangkok temple is known as the Temple of Dawn?
questions.fact: Wat Arun, the Temple of Dawn, is on our riverside sightseeing route.

questions.question: Which river is central to today’s Bangkok boat excursion?
questions.fact: We travel to River City on the Chao Phraya before crossing to Wat Arun and exploring the canals.

questions.question: What does the Thai word khlong refer to?
questions.fact: Khlong, also written klong, means canal; Bangkok’s waterways once formed a major transport network.

questions.question: What nickname reflects old Bangkok’s network of canals?
questions.fact: Bangkok’s extensive canal network helped earn it the nickname Venice of the East.

questions.question: Which temple houses the Emerald Buddha?
questions.fact: Wat Phra Kaew, the Temple of the Emerald Buddha, is within the Grand Palace complex.

questions.question: Despite its name, the Emerald Buddha is carved from what kind of material?
questions.fact: The Emerald Buddha is carved from green stone, commonly described as jade, rather than emerald gemstone.

questions.question: Which temple on our itinerary is famous for a giant reclining Buddha?
questions.fact: Wat Pho, also written Wat Po, is famous for its large reclining Buddha and its association with traditional Thai massage.

questions.question: What vehicle carries us through Bangkok between today’s temple visits?
questions.fact: The itinerary includes a tuk-tuk ride between the Grand Palace visit and Wat Pho.

questions.question: Which city is the final stop on our tour?
questions.fact: Our journey ends in Bangkok after exploring its river, canals, temples and Grand Palace.

questions.question: Which three countries have we visited on this tour?
questions.fact: Our route runs through Vietnam, Cambodia and Thailand, ending in Bangkok.

questions.question: Which country on our route is home to both Angkor Wat and Tonle Sap?
questions.fact: Our Siem Reap stay in Cambodia includes Angkor Wat and a boat excursion on Tonle Sap.

questions.question: Which pair of capitals bookends our journey?
questions.fact: We begin in Hanoi, Vietnam’s capital, and finish in Bangkok, Thailand’s capital.
